vignette:
Patient: Marcus, 47, Bus Driver

Marcus arrives for his sessions straight from the depot, still wearing his blue uniform shirt, the faint smell of diesel and coffee clinging to the fabric. He is a large man with a quiet, deliberate way of moving, as if he is constantly aware of the space he occupies. He sits on the edge of the chair, hands resting on his knees, and his eyes—watchful, gray—scan the room once before settling on a fixed point on the carpet.

He tells the story in fragments, like pieces of a shattered windshield.

The event happened three years ago, on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. Marcus was driving his regular route through the east end of the city, a stretch of road lined with old brick buildings and discount stores. The bus was half-full: a mother with a stroller, two elderly women heading to the pharmacy, a teenager with headphones. It was a routine run, the kind he had done thousands of times over twenty-two years.

At the next stop, a man boarded. Marcus remembers his jacket—a dark hoodie, hood up despite the mild weather. The man walked past the fare box without paying. Marcus called out, his voice even, practiced: "Sir, you need to tap your card or pay the fare." The man turned. His eyes were wide, unfocused. He reached into his jacket and pulled out a knife.

Marcus’s training kicked in. He did not scream. He did not run. He calmly told the passengers to exit through the rear doors, and he opened the front door for the man. "It's okay," he said, his voice steady. "You can go. No one's going to hurt you." The man stared at him for a long, terrible moment—Marcus still sees that stare in the dark of his bedroom—and then he dropped the knife and walked away. The police arrived ten minutes later. They took Marcus’s statement, thanked him for his composure, and told him he had handled it perfectly.

But the composure did not last.

That night, Marcus could not sleep. He lay in his small apartment, staring at the ceiling, his heart pounding as if he were still on the bus. The next morning, he drove his route again. He had to. It was what he did. But at the same stop, the same hour, his hands began to shake. He could not catch his breath. He pulled over, told dispatch he was sick, and sat in the driver's seat for twenty minutes, gripping the wheel until his knuckles were white.

He has not missed a day of work since. But every shift is a battle. He avoids that particular street, rerouting through side streets even if it makes him late. He checks his rearview mirror obsessively, scanning for hoodies, for anyone who boards without meeting his eyes. He has memorized the faces of his regulars, and when a stranger gets on, his throat tightens. He keeps a small can of pepper spray in his lunch bag now, though he has never used it and prays he never will.

At home, Marcus lives a narrow life. His apartment is neat, almost stark. He eats the same meals—frozen dinners, toast, coffee. He has not dated in years. His closest friend is a fellow driver named Dave, but Marcus has stopped joining him for a beer after shifts. The bar is too loud, too crowded. He feels the presence of people behind him like a physical weight. He sleeps in fits, waking from dreams where the man with the knife is not a stranger but someone he knows, someone who whispers his name.

He told me once, in a low voice, that the worst part is not the fear. It is the shame. He was a bus driver. He was supposed to be safe. He was supposed to be in control. And now, every time he hears a siren, his stomach drops. Every time a police car passes his bus, he flinches, waiting for something to happen. He knows the officers are there to help. But his body does not believe it.

He is still driving. Every day. He gets on the bus, he starts the engine, and he goes. But the world he drives through is not the same one he knew before that Tuesday in October. It is a world full of doorways where a man with a knife could appear, a world where the safest place—the driver's seat—feels like a cage.
